screens.title: Combinational Logic: Multiplexers & Demultiplexers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how multiplexers and demultiplexers let a circuit choose and route data without memory. We start with the 2-to-1 multiplexer, a small digital switch that selects one of two inputs based on a selection bit, and the inverse device, the demultiplexer, which sends a single input to one of several outputs. You will see how to implement these with basic gates and how to scale them: build 4-way and 8-way versions by composing smaller Muxes, and create multi-bit versions that operate across an entire data bus. A concrete use case is selecting which register drives the ALU or routing a value to the correct memory destination. Throughout, focus on selection bits: they determine which path is active and are broadcast for multi-bit versions so every bit is chosen consistently. Watch for a common misconception: selection is not data-dependent processing — it is routing. By the end you will be able to write HDL for Mux, Mux16, Mux4Way16 and DMux variants, draw their internal block structure, and explain why recursive construction is the most efficient approach. Consider where large numbers of Muxes appear inside a C P U — that is the practical payoff of these small designs.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Combinational Logic

Multiplexers & Demultiplexers

Build digital switches to route single-bit and multi-bit data using selection bits.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Design Mux/DMux and scale them to buses

Learn the Boolean forms, HDL implementations, and recursive construction patterns that let you compose wider selectors from 2-way components.

Why it matters
Routing is everywhere in a CPU

Registers, ALU inputs, and memory buses rely on many small Muxes working in parallel to choose data paths at clock boundaries.

Outcome
Write and test HDL for Mux family

By the end you will implement Mux, DMux, Mux16 and their wider variants, and explain the selection bit strategy used across all bits.

How we'll learn
Small examples, composition, and bus parallelism

We will combine gates to build a Mux, then compose Muxes into wider selectors and replicate them across buses for multi-bit operation.

Explore Key Topics
Mux & Boolean
Recursive Builds
Multi-bit Buses

These topics explain how a single-bit selector becomes a scalable routing network used across data buses in a computer.

Visual
Train switch metaphor: choose track
Parallel tracks for multi-bit

Multi-bit

Second, you will learn to create wider multiplexers such as 4-way and 8-way by composing 2-way Muxes hierarchically, and understand the selection-bit patterns required for hierarchical choice. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on verification, HDL practice, and reasoning about efficiency. You will learn how to draw block diagrams that use smaller Mux and DMux chips to implement wider versions; this gives a correct-by-construction approach rather than redesigning the logic from scratch. You will implement HDL chips such as Mux16 and Mux4Way16 by instantiating many 1-bit components in parallel and broadcasting selection bits. For hands-on practice, you will run the provided test scripts that exercise each selection pattern across all bits and all inputs, and you will inspect intermediate signals when a test fails. An important verification habit is to check both the selection bits and the data lines independently so you can distinguish routing errors from data errors. You will also reason why a 4-way selector requires three 2-way Muxes — the hierarchical pattern reduces redundancy. Finally, reflect on performance trade-offs: parallel multi-bit selection is simple and fast because all bits are chosen simultaneously. These verification skills ensure that your chips behave identically for every bit of data.

screens.title: Combinational Logic Recap
screens.narratorSegment: Combinational logic produces outputs that depend only on current input values; there is no memory or state. This matters because it makes Mux and DMux predictable functions: given inputs and selection bits, the outputs are uniquely determined. A clear way to see this is with the Mux Boolean expression: output equals a AND NOT sel OR b AND sel. That expression is a pure Boolean formula. As a concrete example, if a equals 1, b equals 0 and sel equals 0, the output is 1 — that follows directly from the expression, and it will remain 1 as long as those inputs do. A common misconception is to think that selection transforms data; it does not. Selection routes a chosen signal unchanged. In practice you implement a Mux by composing Not, And, and Or gates, or by using NAND-only constructions, but the logical function remains stateless. When you build a multi-bit Mux such as Mux16, you replicate the same 1-bit combinational function across each bus line. Each bit's output is a function only of its corresponding data bits and the shared selection bits. That parallelism preserves combinational behavior while scaling the width. Consider how test scripts exploit statelessness: a single vector of inputs maps to a single output vector deterministically. Reflect: when verifying a Mux, which should you check first — the selection bit timing or the data lines — and why?

keyIdea.title: Combinational rule
keyIdea.text: Mux/DMux are stateless boolean functions: outputs are direct functions of current inputs and selection bits, not past signals.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Combinational Logic
Definition

Combinational circuits

Outputs depend only on current inputs. No storage or state appears in the function.

Concrete example
If a=1, b=0, sel=0, then Mux output=1 by the equation: (a AND NOT sel) OR (b AND sel). This result is deterministic for that input combination.
Misconception
Selection is not computation. It routes a chosen signal; it does not modify the routed data bits.
Why this matters
Determinism makes testing straightforward: one input vector maps to one output vector—ideal for automated test scripts.
Teaching Visual
Boolean form
Mux(a, b, sel) = (a && !sel) || (b && sel)
Implementation uses Not, And, and Or gates. For the Mux16 you replicate this 16 times with the same sel broadcast to every bit.
Key Takeaway

Because each bit is independent, multi-bit selectors are parallel replications of the 1-bit boolean function.

screens.title: 2-to-1 Multiplexer — Function and HDL
screens.narratorSegment: A 2-to-1 multiplexer selects between two inputs a and b using a single selection bit. Formally, out equals a when sel is 0 and b when sel is 1. The Boolean expression captures this cleanly: out equals a AND NOT sel OR b AND sel. Translating this to HDL gives a clear structure: first compute notSel, then form aAndNotSel and bAndSel with And gates, and finally Or them. A concrete HDL example makes this tangible. When you write the chip, include the Not, And, and Or parts exactly as shown and ensure signal names match. As an example scenario, imagine selecting either the left register value or the right register value to drive the ALU input based on a control signal; the Mux simply forwards the chosen register bits. A misconception to avoid is combining selection and data values into a single malformed expression — keep selection logic separate and explicit. While NAND-only implementations are possible, using readable gate parts in HDL is clearer for learning. When you test your Mux, exercise both sel values with both input combinations, checking that the output always equals the chosen input. What simple test vector will you start with to verify both branches?

keyIdea.title: Mux formula
keyIdea.text: Mux(a,b,sel) = (a ∧ ¬sel) ∨ (b ∧ sel); implement with Not, And, And, Or in HDL and test both selection branches.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › 2-to-1 Mux
Function

Select between a and b

If sel=0, out=a; if sel=1, out=b. This routing is stateless and deterministic.

Boolean
Mux(a, b, sel) = (a && !sel) || (b && sel)
Example
Selecting which register value feeds the ALU based on a control signal. The Mux forwards the chosen register bits unchanged.
Common mistake
Mixing selection logic into data expressions. Keep selection as gating signals that control which data path is active.
HDL Walkthrough
The HDL uses Not, And, And, Or parts to implement the expression. Below is the reference implementation you will create and test in the simulator.
CHIP Mux {
    IN a, b, sel;
    OUT out;

    PARTS:
    Not(in=sel, out=notSel);
    And(a=a, b=notSel, out=aAndNotSel);
    And(a=b, b=sel, out=bAndSel);
    Or(a=aAndNotSel, b=bAndSel, out=out);
}
Key Takeaway

Implement Mux using explicit gates and test both sel=0 and sel=1 with varied data to confirm routing.

screens.title: Building a 4-way Mux from 2-way Muxes
screens.narratorSegment: A 4-way multiplexer selects one of four input lines using two selection bits. The efficient composition uses three 2-to-1 Muxes arranged in two levels. At the first level you use two 2-way Muxes to pairwise select between a and b, and between c and d, both controlled by the lower-order selection bit. Those two intermediate outputs are then fed into a final 2-way Mux controlled by the higher-order selection bit to choose between the pairs. Concretely, if sel[1] is the high bit and sel[0] is the low bit, you compute Mux(a,b,sel[0]) and Mux(c,d,sel[0]) and then Mux of those results with sel[1]. This hierarchical approach requires three 2-way Muxes, not four, because the first level reduces four candidates to two, and the second level reduces two to one. As an example, if sel[1..0] = 10, the final Mux will pick the intermediate result coming from the c/d pair, and within that pair sel[0] dictates which of c or d was chosen earlier. A common misunderstanding is to try to implement a 4-way Mux by naïvely wiring four And/Or terms; composition using smaller Mux chips yields clearer HDL and reduces wiring complexity. When implementing in HDL, instantiate three Mux parts and wire the selection bits precisely; the pattern generalizes recursively to 8-way Muxes and beyond. After building, test every two-bit selection value to confirm correct routing for all four inputs.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchical pattern
keyIdea.text: Use two first-level Muxes to narrow four inputs to two, then a third Mux to pick the final output; selection bits control levels hierarchically.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › 4-way Mux
Process

Compose 4-way from 2-way parts

Build two Muxes to select pairs, then a third to choose between those results using hierarchical selection bits.

Step 1
Create left = Mux(a,b,sel0) and right = Mux(c,d,sel0).
Step 2
Output = Mux(left, right, sel1). Sel1 chooses the pair, sel0 chooses inside each pair.
Example
For sel[1..0] = 10, sel1=1 picks the right pair, and sel0=0 picks c within that pair.
Visual Steps
1
First-level pairwise selection reduces the candidate set from four to two.
2
Second-level selection uses the high-order select bit to pick between intermediate results.
3
This pattern recurses: an 8-way uses two 4-way Muxes plus a 2-way Mux to choose between them.
Check your understanding

Why are three Muxes sufficient for 4 inputs? Answer: two reduce 4→2, the third reduces 2→1.

screens.title: Demultiplexer — The Inverse Router
screens.narratorSegment: A demultiplexer routes a single input to one of multiple outputs based on a selection bit. For the 1-to-2 DMux, the input in is routed to output a when sel is 0, and to output b when sel is 1. The Boolean expressions are simple: a equals in AND NOT sel, and b equals in AND sel. This means the DMux gates the input onto exactly one output or onto none if the input is zero. A concrete example: if a control signal must enable one of two devices, the DMux sends the enable to the selected device and leaves the other inactive. When you implement a DMux in HDL, use Not and And gates to generate a and b and ensure no collisions occur — only one output line should carry the input at a time. A common mistake is misunderstanding DMux as distributing copies of data to multiple lines; it does not copy except when selection indicates the same destination. For wider demultiplexers the same composition idea applies: use smaller DMuxes in a tree to route to many outputs. Closing question: when debugging a DMux that drives hardware, why is it important to confirm inactive outputs are zero and not floating?

keyIdea.title: DMux basics
keyIdea.text: DMux gates the input onto one output based on sel: a = in ∧ ¬sel, b = in ∧ sel. Use Not and And gates to avoid output collisions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Demultiplexer
Definition

1-to-2 DMux

Route one input to exactly one of two outputs based on a selection bit.

Boolean
a = in && !sel
b = in && sel
Example
Send a control pulse to exactly one of two devices. If in=1 and sel=1, then b=1 and a=0.
Pitfall
Ensure inactive outputs are driven low. Floating outputs lead to indeterminate hardware behavior.
Composition
You can build 1-to-4 DMux by combining three 1-to-2 DMuxes in a similar hierarchical pattern used for Muxes; this recursively expands routing to more outputs.
Key Takeaway

DMux duplicates the selection logic on the input and gates it to exclusive outputs; composition gives wider routing trees.

screens.title: Scaling to 8-way and the Recursive Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Wider multiplexers follow a recursive structure: a 2^n-way Mux can be composed from two 2^(n-1)-way Muxes plus one 2-way Mux. For example, an 8-way Mux uses two 4-way Muxes to pick among the first and second halves, and a final 2-way Mux to choose which half's result is forwarded, controlled by the highest-order selection bit. The selection bits are arranged so that lower-order bits decide inside each half, while higher-order bits pick the half. This recursive pattern reduces design complexity and clarifies HDL: you implement the smaller Muxes once and reuse them. A concrete construction step: implement Mux4Way for each half, then instantiate Mux to choose between their outputs using the top selection bit. A common misconception is thinking that adding more inputs requires exponentially more unique gate formulas; in reality, hierarchical composition scales linearly in the number of component blocks and selection bits increase logarithmically. For DMux the inverse tree pattern applies: use a 1-to-2 DMux to split the signal, then feed each branch into a 1-to-4 DMux to produce a 1-to-8 routing. When you write HDL for these recursive chips, wire selection slices carefully so each submodule receives the correct selection bits. After building, verify every selection vector to ensure the hierarchical mapping is correct. Where would this recursion stop in practical hardware design?

keyIdea.title: Recursive scaling
keyIdea.text: Construct 2^n-way selectors by composing two 2^(n-1)-way selectors and one 2-way Mux; selection bits map hierarchically.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Recursive Mux
Pattern

2^n-way by composition

Use two smaller selectors and a top-level Mux to choose between their outputs. Selection bits are partitioned by level.

8-way example
left = Mux4Way(inputs[0..3], sel[0..1]) right = Mux4Way(inputs[4..7], sel[0..1]) out = Mux(left, right, sel[2])
Why it helps
Modularity simplifies HDL and reduces chances of wiring errors. It also mirrors efficient hardware practice.
Checklist
  • Partition selection bits by level (low-order for inner Muxes).
  • Instantiate smaller chips, wire intermediate outputs to top-level Mux.
  • Test every selection vector to validate the hierarchical mapping.
Common misconception

You do not need unique gate formulas for each wider Mux; composition reuses smaller, tested building blocks.

screens.title: Multi-bit Mux: Mux16 Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: A multi-bit Mux applies the same 1-bit selection to each line of a bus. The Mux16 chip is simply 16 independent Muxes with identical sel. The HDL shows repeated instantiations for each bit index, for example Mux(a=a[0], b=b[0], sel=sel, out=out[0]) and so on up to index 15. Because each bit is chosen independently, testing is straightforward: set sel to 0 and confirm out matches a across all 16 bits; set sel to 1 and confirm out matches b. This parallel replication is the key idea — selection is broadcast to all component Muxes. An important advantage is predictable timing: all bits are selected simultaneously, so the bus changes consistently. A common error when coding Mux16 is miswiring indices or accidentally tying sel to a single bit of a component rather than broadcasting it. When you write the HDL, follow a consistent pattern for part instances and verify wiring visually before running tests. Example HDL fragment in the visual area demonstrates the repeated instantiation pattern you will use in the simulator. After implementation, design test vectors that exercise mixed-bit patterns to confirm the broadcast selection behaves as expected across the entire bus.

keyIdea.title: Bus parallelism
keyIdea.text: Mux16 is 16 parallel 1-bit Muxes sharing the same selection bit; this guarantees simultaneous, consistent routing across the bus.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Mux16
Concept

Parallel 1-bit Muxes

Broadcast the same sel to 16 1-bit Mux instances so each bit is selected independently but at the same time.

Why parallelism helps
Parallel replication is straightforward, aligns with hardware fanout, and makes testing simple.
Common bug
Indexing errors: wiring a[1] to out[0] or accidentally creating mismatched bit connections.
HDL Pattern
CHIP Mux16 {
    IN a[16], b[16], sel;
    OUT out[16];

    PARTS:
    Mux(a=a[0], b=b[0], sel=sel, out=out[0]);
    Mux(a=a[1], b=b[1], sel=sel, out=out[1]);
    ...
    Mux(a=a[15], b=b[15], sel=sel, out=out[15]);
}
Key Takeaway

Broadcast the selection bit to all 1-bit Muxes and verify with test vectors that check all bits under both selection values.

screens.title: DMux4Way and DMux8Way Construction
screens.narratorSegment: Constructing wider DMuxes mirrors Mux recursion but in reverse: a 1-to-4 DMux uses three 1-to-2 DMuxes. First split the input with a top-level 1-to-2 DMux controlled by the high-order selection bit, producing two branches. Then send each branch into a lower-level 1-to-2 DMux controlled by the low-order bit. For example, to build a 1-to-4 DMux, route in through DMux(in, sel1) to create leftBranch and rightBranch, then DMux each branch with sel0 to produce four outputs. For a 1-to-8 DMux, extend the tree: use a 1-to-2 DMux at the top, two 1-to-4 DMuxes below, or equivalently cascade further 1-to-2 splits. A concrete scenario: routing a single write-enable to one of many register units — the DMux ensures only the targeted register receives the enable. Watch for the common error of not inverting the right selection bit for the lower-level DMux parts; selection bits must be aligned to the correct tree level. When testing a DMux, confirm that exactly one output carries the input for every selection vector and that inactive outputs are zero. This pattern generalizes cleanly and makes HDL straightforward to write by reusing the smaller DMux modules you already implemented.

keyIdea.title: DMux tree
keyIdea.text: Use a tree of 1-to-2 DMuxes to route one input into many outputs; test each selection to ensure exclusivity and correct zeroing of unused lines.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › DMux Tree
Pattern

1-to-4 from 1-to-2 parts

Split the input, then split each branch again. Selection bits choose the branch hierarchy.

Step example
Top: DMux(in, sel1) → left, right. Then DMux(left, sel0) → out0,out1; DMux(right, sel0) → out2,out3.
Verification
For each sel pair, exactly one out should equal in and all others must be zero.
Practical note

DMux trees drive control lines to many modules. Ensure fanout and signal integrity when routing enables in actual hardware designs.

Key Takeaway

DMux composition mirrors Mux recursion in reverse; build larger routers by reusing tested 1-to-2 DMux units.

screens.title: Mux vs DMux — Roles and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Multiplexers and demultiplexers are complementary. A Mux selects between multiple data sources and forwards the chosen source to a single consumer. A DMux takes a single source and routes it to one of many destinations. Use a Mux when you need to choose which register or memory cell supplies data to a shared consumer, such as selecting ALU inputs. Use a DMux when a single controller signal must be delivered to one of many units, for example routing a write-enable to one targeted register. A concrete scenario: when reading from registers, a Mux chooses which register's value goes to the ALU. Conversely, when writing, a DMux routes the write-enable so only the chosen register updates. A common confusion is to think of DMux as just a Mux reversed; while conceptually inverse, their HDL implementations and test patterns differ — Mux composes data selects, DMux composes gated distribution. Both scale by the same recursion pattern and both can be implemented as multi-bit versions by parallel replication. Closing thought: identify a read and write path in a simple C P U and point out where Muxes and DMuxes appear and why they are necessary.

keyIdea.text: Mux chooses among sources for a single consumer; DMux directs a single source to one of many destinations. Both scale by composition and parallel replication.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Mux vs DMux
Mux

Select a source

Choose which input feeds a shared consumer using selection bits.

Use case
Selecting register value to drive an ALU input.
Testing
Verify every sel value and that out equals the selected input for all bits in multi-bit versions.
DMux

Route to a destination

Take one input and send it to exactly one chosen output line based on selection bits.

Use case
Send a write-enable to a single register when writing data to register file.
Testing
Confirm exactly one output equals the input for each selection vector; others must be zero.
Reflection
Scan a simple CPU datapath and mark where source selection and destination routing are required. Those are the places Muxes and DMuxes live.

screens.title: Hands-on: Chips to Build and Test
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity lists concrete chips to implement and test in the Hardware Simulator. Start with Mux and DMux to familiarize yourself with parts and testing. Then implement Mux16 and DMux16 by creating parallel 1-bit instances and broadcasting selection bits; write test scripts that confirm the entire bus behaves correctly when sel toggles. Next build Mux4Way16 and Mux8Way16 using the recursive composition pattern: assemble smaller multi-bit Muxes and wire the selection slices properly. For DMux4Way and DMux8Way, construct trees of DMux parts to route an input across many destinations. When testing, design vectors that exercise all selection combinations and check every bit simultaneously. A practical verification tip is to test boundary cases like all-zero and all-one inputs and mixed patterns; these catch wiring and index errors. Also, for multi-bit chips, include tests that pass different patterns on a and b to ensure bits are not cross-wired. Finally, when a test fails, inspect intermediate signals such as the outputs of first-level Muxes to isolate whether a wiring or logic error occurred. This step-by-step approach reduces debugging time and ensures correctness across the full chip family.

screens.title: Assessment: Why three Muxes for a 4-way?
screens.narratorSegment: A typical assessment asks: why does a 4-way Mux use three 2-way Muxes and not four? The answer is hierarchical reduction. Two first-level Muxes each reduce two inputs to one intermediate result, so 4 inputs become 2. The third Mux then selects between those two intermediates. This requires only three Muxes because each level halves the candidate set. Using four 2-way Muxes would be redundant and would not implement the correct selection semantics without additional wiring and control. A concrete reasoning example: label inputs a,b,c,d and selection bits sel1 (high) and sel0 (low). The first-level Muxes compute left=Mux(a,b,sel0) and right=Mux(c,d,sel0). The top-level Mux outputs Mux(left,right,sel1). If you tried four Muxes in parallel you would need extra gates to combine their outputs and you would not naturally map the two-bit selection vector correctly. This hierarchical pattern generalizes: for 2^n inputs you need 2^n - 1 two-way Muxes arranged as a binary tree, reusing smaller Mux blocks reduces design complexity and testing surface. Closing prompt: sketch the instantiation list for Mux4Way in HDL and check how selection bits are passed to each instance.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Assessment

Why three Muxes implement a 4-way selector

Hierarchical reduction is the explanation: two Muxes reduce four inputs to two, the third reduces two to one.

Structure
left = Mux(a,b,sel0) right = Mux(c,d,sel0) out = Mux(left,right,sel1)
Efficiency
Three Muxes avoid redundancy and map selection bits cleanly. Using four Muxes would require extra combining logic.
Reflect

Can you generalize how many two-way Muxes are needed for 8 inputs? Think about the binary tree node count.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Remember these concise ideas as you implement and test your chips. First, combinational logic is stateless: outputs are strict functions of current inputs. Multiplexers are selectors that forward one of many inputs to a single output under control of selection bits. Demultiplexers do the inverse: they route one input to a single selected output. Second, wider selectors and demultiplexers follow a recursive composition pattern: build a 2^n-way unit from two 2^(n-1)-way units and a 2-way selector. This hierarchical pattern reduces wiring complexity and eases HDL instantiation. Third, multi-bit versions are parallel replications of 1-bit units: a Mux16 is just sixteen 1-bit Muxes sharing the same selection bit. Testing strategies should exercise all selection vectors and check intermediate signals when failures occur. Keep in mind the practical roles: Muxes choose sources, DMuxes route to destinations, and together they form the routing fabric inside CPUs. Which of these key ideas will you use first in your HDL work?

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: As a final review, keep three compact lessons in your head. First, selection bits are control signals that determine routing; always ensure they are broadcast correctly for multi-bit chips. Second, reuse: hierarchical composition of 2-way units is the standard method to build 4-way, 8-way, and larger selectors; this keeps HDL modular and reduces errors. Third, parallel replication is the right approach for buses — each bit is selected independently but simultaneously. When you move to debugging, verify selection signals and intermediate results before blaming data sources. These simple rules will make your HDL implementations correct and easier to test. Which of these rules will you apply first when building your Mux16 or DMux8Way? What to Remember means broadcast selection, compose recursively, and replicate for buses — these three rules make routing designs reliable and testable.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What to Remember
Broadcast selection
Ensure the same sel line reaches every parallel 1-bit Mux in a bus.
Compose recursively
Build wide selectors from smaller ones to keep designs modular.
Replicate for buses
Multi-bit chips are parallel copies of 1-bit logic operating synchronously.
One-line summary

Mux and DMux are the routing primitives of a CPU: compose, broadcast, and test thoroughly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how multiplexers and demultiplexers let a circuit choose and route data without memory. We start with the 2-to-1 multiplexer, a small digital switch that selects one of two inputs based on a selection bit, and the inverse device, the demultiplexer, which sends a single input to one of several outputs. You will see how to implement these with basic gates and how to scale them: build 4-way and 8-way versions by composing smaller Muxes, and create multi-bit versions that operate across an entire data bus. A concrete use case is selecting which register drives the ALU or routing a value to the correct memory destination. Throughout, focus on selection bits: they determine which path is active and are broadcast for multi-bit versions so every bit is chosen consistently. Watch for a common misconception: selection is not data-dependent processing — it is routing. By the end you will be able to write HDL for Mux, Mux16, Mux4Way16 and DMux variants, draw their internal block structure, and explain why recursive construction is the most efficient approach. Consider where large numbers of Muxes appear inside a C P U — that is the practical payoff of these small designs.

In the next screens you will build practical skills for designing, composing, and scaling multiplexers and demultiplexers. First, you will learn to design and implement a 2-to-1 multiplexer and its inverse using gates and HDL. This matters because a Mux is a core selector in many C P U datapaths; for example, deciding which register drives the ALU inputs. Second, you will learn to create wider multiplexers such as 4-way and 8-way by composing 2-way Muxes hierarchically, and understand the selection-bit patterns required for hierarchical choice. Third, you will practice building demultiplexers that route a single input to multiple outputs, which is essential for sending control or data signals to the correct destination. Finally, you will implement multi-bit versions where the same selection bit controls many parallel 1-bit units, which is how real buses operate. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic or small visualization to keep the relationships clear, and a competency milestone to verify your work in the simulator. As you progress, think about the difference between routing and computation: selection routes data without transforming it. How will you test that your selection logic routes every bit correctly?

This second objectives screen focuses on verification, HDL practice, and reasoning about efficiency. You will learn how to draw block diagrams that use smaller Mux and DMux chips to implement wider versions; this gives a correct-by-construction approach rather than redesigning the logic from scratch. You will implement HDL chips such as Mux16 and Mux4Way16 by instantiating many 1-bit components in parallel and broadcasting selection bits. For hands-on practice, you will run the provided test scripts that exercise each selection pattern across all bits and all inputs, and you will inspect intermediate signals when a test fails. An important verification habit is to check both the selection bits and the data lines independently so you can distinguish routing errors from data errors. You will also reason why a 4-way selector requires three 2-way Muxes — the hierarchical pattern reduces redundancy. Finally, reflect on performance trade-offs: parallel multi-bit selection is simple and fast because all bits are chosen simultaneously. These verification skills ensure that your chips behave identically for every bit of data.

Combinational logic produces outputs that depend only on current input values; there is no memory or state. This matters because it makes Mux and DMux predictable functions: given inputs and selection bits, the outputs are uniquely determined. A clear way to see this is with the Mux Boolean expression: output equals a AND NOT sel OR b AND sel. That expression is a pure Boolean formula. As a concrete example, if a equals 1, b equals 0 and sel equals 0, the output is 1 — that follows directly from the expression, and it will remain 1 as long as those inputs do. A common misconception is to think that selection transforms data; it does not. Selection routes a chosen signal unchanged. In practice you implement a Mux by composing Not, And, and Or gates, or by using NAND-only constructions, but the logical function remains stateless. When you build a multi-bit Mux such as Mux16, you replicate the same 1-bit combinational function across each bus line. Each bit's output is a function only of its corresponding data bits and the shared selection bits. That parallelism preserves combinational behavior while scaling the width. Consider how test scripts exploit statelessness: a single vector of inputs maps to a single output vector deterministically. Reflect: when verifying a Mux, which should you check first — the selection bit timing or the data lines — and why?

A 2-to-1 multiplexer selects between two inputs a and b using a single selection bit. Formally, out equals a when sel is 0 and b when sel is 1. The Boolean expression captures this cleanly: out equals a AND NOT sel OR b AND sel. Translating this to HDL gives a clear structure: first compute notSel, then form aAndNotSel and bAndSel with And gates, and finally Or them. A concrete HDL example makes this tangible. When you write the chip, include the Not, And, and Or parts exactly as shown and ensure signal names match. As an example scenario, imagine selecting either the left register value or the right register value to drive the ALU input based on a control signal; the Mux simply forwards the chosen register bits. A misconception to avoid is combining selection and data values into a single malformed expression — keep selection logic separate and explicit. While NAND-only implementations are possible, using readable gate parts in HDL is clearer for learning. When you test your Mux, exercise both sel values with both input combinations, checking that the output always equals the chosen input. What simple test vector will you start with to verify both branches?

A 4-way multiplexer selects one of four input lines using two selection bits. The efficient composition uses three 2-to-1 Muxes arranged in two levels. At the first level you use two 2-way Muxes to pairwise select between a and b, and between c and d, both controlled by the lower-order selection bit. Those two intermediate outputs are then fed into a final 2-way Mux controlled by the higher-order selection bit to choose between the pairs. Concretely, if sel[1] is the high bit and sel[0] is the low bit, you compute Mux(a,b,sel[0]) and Mux(c,d,sel[0]) and then Mux of those results with sel[1]. This hierarchical approach requires three 2-way Muxes, not four, because the first level reduces four candidates to two, and the second level reduces two to one. As an example, if sel[1..0] = 10, the final Mux will pick the intermediate result coming from the c/d pair, and within that pair sel[0] dictates which of c or d was chosen earlier. A common misunderstanding is to try to implement a 4-way Mux by naïvely wiring four And/Or terms; composition using smaller Mux chips yields clearer HDL and reduces wiring complexity. When implementing in HDL, instantiate three Mux parts and wire the selection bits precisely; the pattern generalizes recursively to 8-way Muxes and beyond. After building, test every two-bit selection value to confirm correct routing for all four inputs.

A demultiplexer routes a single input to one of multiple outputs based on a selection bit. For the 1-to-2 DMux, the input in is routed to output a when sel is 0, and to output b when sel is 1. The Boolean expressions are simple: a equals in AND NOT sel, and b equals in AND sel. This means the DMux gates the input onto exactly one output or onto none if the input is zero. A concrete example: if a control signal must enable one of two devices, the DMux sends the enable to the selected device and leaves the other inactive. When you implement a DMux in HDL, use Not and And gates to generate a and b and ensure no collisions occur — only one output line should carry the input at a time. A common mistake is misunderstanding DMux as distributing copies of data to multiple lines; it does not copy except when selection indicates the same destination. For wider demultiplexers the same composition idea applies: use smaller DMuxes in a tree to route to many outputs. Closing question: when debugging a DMux that drives hardware, why is it important to confirm inactive outputs are zero and not floating?

Wider multiplexers follow a recursive structure: a 2^n-way Mux can be composed from two 2^(n-1)-way Muxes plus one 2-way Mux. For example, an 8-way Mux uses two 4-way Muxes to pick among the first and second halves, and a final 2-way Mux to choose which half's result is forwarded, controlled by the highest-order selection bit. The selection bits are arranged so that lower-order bits decide inside each half, while higher-order bits pick the half. This recursive pattern reduces design complexity and clarifies HDL: you implement the smaller Muxes once and reuse them. A concrete construction step: implement Mux4Way for each half, then instantiate Mux to choose between their outputs using the top selection bit. A common misconception is thinking that adding more inputs requires exponentially more unique gate formulas; in reality, hierarchical composition scales linearly in the number of component blocks and selection bits increase logarithmically. For DMux the inverse tree pattern applies: use a 1-to-2 DMux to split the signal, then feed each branch into a 1-to-4 DMux to produce a 1-to-8 routing. When you write HDL for these recursive chips, wire selection slices carefully so each submodule receives the correct selection bits. After building, verify every selection vector to ensure the hierarchical mapping is correct. Where would this recursion stop in practical hardware design?

A multi-bit Mux applies the same 1-bit selection to each line of a bus. The Mux16 chip is simply 16 independent Muxes with identical sel. The HDL shows repeated instantiations for each bit index, for example Mux(a=a[0], b=b[0], sel=sel, out=out[0]) and so on up to index 15. Because each bit is chosen independently, testing is straightforward: set sel to 0 and confirm out matches a across all 16 bits; set sel to 1 and confirm out matches b. This parallel replication is the key idea — selection is broadcast to all component Muxes. An important advantage is predictable timing: all bits are selected simultaneously, so the bus changes consistently. A common error when coding Mux16 is miswiring indices or accidentally tying sel to a single bit of a component rather than broadcasting it. When you write the HDL, follow a consistent pattern for part instances and verify wiring visually before running tests. Example HDL fragment in the visual area demonstrates the repeated instantiation pattern you will use in the simulator. After implementation, design test vectors that exercise mixed-bit patterns to confirm the broadcast selection behaves as expected across the entire bus.

Constructing wider DMuxes mirrors Mux recursion but in reverse: a 1-to-4 DMux uses three 1-to-2 DMuxes. First split the input with a top-level 1-to-2 DMux controlled by the high-order selection bit, producing two branches. Then send each branch into a lower-level 1-to-2 DMux controlled by the low-order bit. For example, to build a 1-to-4 DMux, route in through DMux(in, sel1) to create leftBranch and rightBranch, then DMux each branch with sel0 to produce four outputs. For a 1-to-8 DMux, extend the tree: use a 1-to-2 DMux at the top, two 1-to-4 DMuxes below, or equivalently cascade further 1-to-2 splits. A concrete scenario: routing a single write-enable to one of many register units — the DMux ensures only the targeted register receives the enable. Watch for the common error of not inverting the right selection bit for the lower-level DMux parts; selection bits must be aligned to the correct tree level. When testing a DMux, confirm that exactly one output carries the input for every selection vector and that inactive outputs are zero. This pattern generalizes cleanly and makes HDL straightforward to write by reusing the smaller DMux modules you already implemented.

Multiplexers and demultiplexers are complementary. A Mux selects between multiple data sources and forwards the chosen source to a single consumer. A DMux takes a single source and routes it to one of many destinations. Use a Mux when you need to choose which register or memory cell supplies data to a shared consumer, such as selecting ALU inputs. Use a DMux when a single controller signal must be delivered to one of many units, for example routing a write-enable to one targeted register. A concrete scenario: when reading from registers, a Mux chooses which register's value goes to the ALU. Conversely, when writing, a DMux routes the write-enable so only the chosen register updates. A common confusion is to think of DMux as just a Mux reversed; while conceptually inverse, their HDL implementations and test patterns differ — Mux composes data selects, DMux composes gated distribution. Both scale by the same recursion pattern and both can be implemented as multi-bit versions by parallel replication. The hands-on activity lists concrete chips to implement and test in the Hardware Simulator. Start with Mux and DMux to familiarize yourself with parts and testing. A typical assessment asks: why does a 4-way Mux use three 2-way Muxes and not four? The answer is hierarchical reduction. Two first-level Muxes each reduce two inputs to one intermediate result, so 4 inputs become 2. The third Mux then selects between those two intermediates. This requires only three Muxes because each level halves the candidate set. Using four 2-way Muxes would be redundant and would not implement the correct selection semantics without additional wiring and control. A concrete reasoning example: label inputs a,b,c,d and selection bits sel1 (high) and sel0 (low). The first-level Muxes compute left=Mux(a,b,sel0) and right=Mux(c,d,sel0). The top-level Mux outputs Mux(left,right,sel1). If you tried four Muxes in parallel you would need extra gates to combine their outputs and you would not naturally map the two-bit selection vector correctly. This hierarchical pattern generalizes: for 2^n inputs you need 2^n - 1 two-way Muxes arranged as a binary tree, reusing smaller Mux blocks reduces design complexity and testing surface. Remember these concise ideas as you implement and test your chips. First, combinational logic is stateless: outputs are strict functions of current inputs. Multiplexers are selectors that forward one of many inputs to a single output under control of selection bits. Demultiplexers do the inverse: they route one input to a single selected output. Second, wider selectors and demultiplexers follow a recursive composition pattern: build a 2^n-way unit from two 2^(n-1)-way units and a 2-way selector. This hierarchical pattern reduces wiring complexity and eases HDL instantiation. Third, multi-bit versions are parallel replications of 1-bit units: a Mux16 is just sixteen 1-bit Muxes sharing the same selection bit. Testing strategies should exercise all selection vectors and check intermediate signals when failures occur. Keep in mind the practical roles: Muxes choose sources, DMuxes route to destinations, and together they form the routing fabric inside CPUs. As a final review, keep three compact lessons in your head. First, selection bits are control signals that determine routing; always ensure they are broadcast correctly for multi-bit chips. Second, reuse: hierarchical composition of 2-way units is the standard method to build 4-way, 8-way, and larger selectors; this keeps HDL modular and reduces errors. Third, parallel replication is the right approach for buses — each bit is selected independently but simultaneously. When you move to debugging, verify selection signals and intermediate results before blaming data sources. These simple rules will make your HDL implementations correct and easier to test.
